_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a2.1: Gemara. He left him: Rabbi Hoshaya [left] bar Kappara.
rashi:a2.2: He raised a dilemma before him: Rabbi Hoshaya [asked] bar Kappara.
rashi:a2.3: On the night of the eighth: [the eighth] for the first discharge, so that on the next day he would have been fit for an offering.
rashi:a2.4: What do Beit Hillel [say] etc.: does he bring two offerings or not?
rashi:a4.1: The Babylonian: Rabbi Ḥiyya came up from Babylonia, as we say there (Sukka 20a): At first the Torah was forgotten from Israel; Hillel the Babylonian came up and established it. It was forgotten again; the members of the exile came up and established it. And who are they? Yehuda and Ḥizkiyya, the sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya.
rashi:a4.2: Iyya: Rabbi Ḥiyya; he says it to him in a derogatory form.
rashi:a4.3: (Rabbi Hoshaya asked bar Kappara again.) [This line stands in parentheses in the printed Rashi.]
rashi:a4.4: Let us return to the earlier ones: like “the Master said.” Above [it was taught]: “The verse states…” And Rabbi Hoshaya was uncertain whether Beit Hillel’s reason is because of “or for a daughter,” or because they hold that night is not lacking time.
rashi:a5.1: And that which is taught, “he does not bring an offering,” [holds] that night is lacking time: and [according to it] Beit Hillel’s reason is because of “or for a daughter.”
rashi:a6.1: A zav with two sightings: his first discharge was one of two sightings.
rashi:a6.2: Of three: therefore, since the time fit for the offering has not yet come, it is all one long discharge.
rashi:a8.1: Let him teach it: in the second chapter (below, Keritot 9a), with “five bring one offering etc.,” just as it teaches a nazirite who became impure with many impurities.
rashi:a8.2: It is not definitive for him: since sometimes he is liable even for sightings at night, for example, where he saw one on the night of the eighth and two on the following day.
rashi:a9.1: It is merely semen: it carries only impurity until evening, as it is taught: “This is the law of the zav, and of him from whom semen goes out” — a zav at his first sighting was compared to one who had a seminal emission, in tractate Nidda (35a). And they also said in Megilla (8a): two for impurity, and three for an offering as well; but a single sighting carries only impurity until evening.
rashi:a11.1: And does Rabbi Yoḥanan say etc.: since he said, “two at night and one by day etc.”
rashi:a12.1: Became impure: a nazirite, on the eighth day, which is fit for an offering, brings two offerings.
rashi:a12.2: On the night: of the eighth, he does not bring, since with regard to the offering it is one long impurity, as night is lacking time.
rashi:a15.1: Mishna. An uncertain ziva: for example, [a woman who lost count] who saw [blood] for three days and does not know whether it was in her days of menstruation or in her days of ziva. She brings an offering, and it is not eaten.
rashi:a15.2: An uncertain birth: for example, she miscarried and it is not known what [it was].
rashi:a15.3: A woman who has five uncertain births or five uncertain zivot brings one offering: the bird sin offering that comes for an uncertainty.
rashi:a15.4: And she may partake of offerings: since this offering comes for purification, and it is like immersion. If a woman became impure with several impurities, one immersion counts for all of them; this offering is the same.
rashi:a15.5: And the remaining offerings are not an obligation for her: the Sages did not require her to bring them, since even the one they permitted only with difficulty, [as it means] offering on the altar a bird killed by pinching that is perhaps non-sacred; and [they permitted it] because otherwise she would have no remedy to become pure for sacrificial food.
rashi:a15.6: Five definite births or five definite zivot: she brings one offering and partakes of offerings, as I explained.
rashi:a15.7: And the remaining offerings are an obligation for her: as we say below in the second chapter (Keritot 9b): One might think she brings one offering for both a birth before the completion [of her days] and a birth after the completion; the verse states: “This [is the law]” [Leviticus 12:7].
rashi:a16.2: At a gold dinar: at two gold coins, a nest for a gold dinar.
rashi:a16.4: He entered the court to teach etc.: although he was lenient against the words of the Torah, it was “a time to act for the Lord” [Psalms 119:126]. For if they could not find [birds], they would stop bringing even one, and would eat sacrificial food in bodily impurity.
rashi:a16.5: Nests at rivatayim: two nests for two quarters of a silver dinar. Another version: rivatayim is a term for half.
rashi:a17.1: Gemara. This is our reading in the Tosefta: “five definite births and five uncertain births etc.” [The printed Gemara also has “five definite births and five uncertain discharges.”] Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri says: For the definite: we are concerned for negligence. For if you say she brings it for one of them, perhaps there is a woman who will give birth once, definitely, and will not want to bring an offering, and will say: “Last year I had five definite births and I did not bring an offering for four of them, and now I am to bring one?” And Rabbi Akiva holds: since last year she did not eat without any offering at all, she will not be negligent.
rashi:a17.2: She should say: For the last: “I am bringing it,” and she is exempt from the rest. Rabbi Akiva says: She should say “for one of them,” and need not say “for the last,” and she is exempt from the rest.
rashi:a18.1: And for the definite she should say “for the last” and she is exempt: now, from the obligation of the remaining offerings, and she partakes of offerings today, and tomorrow she will offer the remaining offerings.
rashi:a18.2: If there is a definite one among them: of the same kind as the uncertainty, she says “for the definite,” so that it becomes a definite [offering] and is eaten, and she is entirely exempt; as I explained in the mishna, that they permitted offering an uncertain [bird] only with difficulty.
rashi:a18.3: For one of them: even for the first.
rashi:a18.4: Whether for the definite etc.: she need not say “I am bringing it for the last.” In Rabbi Akiva’s statement we do not read “and she is exempt.” [The Davidson English, following the printed text, includes it.]
rashi:a19.1: Until he brings all of them: it does not atone. If he brought the first sin offering, the other sins still stand. Here too, if she brought for the earlier ones, the last impurity is still in its place, and she is not purified to eat sacrificial food. Therefore she says “for the last,” and is purified, and she brings for the earlier ones later.
rashi:a20.1: One who is obligated in five immersions: even if he said, “I am immersing for the first,” he is purified of every impurity.
tosafot:a8.1: Let him teach it with “five bring”: This is puzzling: how could he teach it with them? This tanna holds that night is lacking time, so it is all one long discharge. And for this very reason we say below, regarding a nazirite who became impure many times, that it cannot be established according to Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], who says that the naziriteship of purity does not take effect until the eighth day, even in a case where he became impure on the night of the eighth; for if night is lacking time, it is all one long impurity. And my teacher says that a zav who sees on the night of the eighth is not comparable to a nazirite who became impure on the night of the eighth. A zav who has counted seven clean days becomes pure immediately, so when he saw again on the night of the eighth, it is another discharge. But for a nazirite, the naziriteship of purity does not take effect until the next day, and night is lacking time, so it is all one long impurity, since he has not yet become pure of the first impurity.
tosafot:a16.1: He entered the court and taught: It seems that he was not lenient against the words of the Torah; rather, he compares it entirely to immersions. For if one is obligated in five immersions, once he has immersed one time he need not immerse again.
tosafot:a19.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri compares it to a sin offering: This is puzzling: if so, what difference is there between the first and the last? On the contrary, she should need to bring all of them, and one nest should not suffice for her.
gershom:a1.1: [The printed text marks: up to here belongs to 7b.] “The verse states: ‘or for a daughter.’” It is superfluous, since it could have said, “And when the days of her purification are fulfilled she shall bring a lamb.” Rather, it was written for this: to include the night of the eighty-first for an offering.
gershom:a2.1: Would regularly: for he was his student.
gershom:a3.1: He left him: he left bar Kappara, and came and learned from Rabbi Ḥiyya, who was greater than bar Kappara.
gershom:a4.1: Encountered him: bar Kappara [encountered] Rabbi Hoshaya.
gershom:a5.1: He raised a dilemma before him: Rabbi Hoshaya [asked]: a zav who saw three sightings on the night of the eighth, at the end of his days of counting. For on the eighth day he must bring an offering for the first discharges; and now that he saw three sightings on the night of the eighth, is he obligated in another offering? What do Beit Hillel say about this matter, etc.
gershom:a6.1: Because the verses are superfluous: “or for a daughter,” as he said. Rabbi Hoshaya did not answer him anything, because he was pained that he called Rabbi Ḥiyya, his teacher, “Iyya,” a derogatory form, and “the Babylonian,” since Rabbi Ḥiyya came up from Babylonia; and he did not want to call him by his name.
gershom:a7.1: He said to him: Rabbi Hoshaya [said to] bar Kappara: We need the words of Iyya, whom you disparage, because he knows how to answer and you do not. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads this line as Rabbi Hoshaya’s reply; the Davidson English gives “Do we require the statement of Iyya?” to bar Kappara.]
gershom:a8.1: Let us return to the earlier ones: the matters they asked. That is, as in “the Master said”: “The verse states, etc.”
gershom:a9.1: What, is it not a dispute of tanna’im, as that which is taught “he brings” holds that night is not lacking time? And that is also the reason for a woman who miscarries on the night of the eighty-first, and no verse is needed.
gershom:a10.1: And that which is taught “he does not bring” holds that night is lacking time, and here, with one who miscarries on the night of the eighty-first, the reason they obligate her is that it is written “or for a daughter.” No: everyone holds that night is lacking time, and they have “or for a daughter” to include the night of the eighty-first. And that which is taught “he brings” is about a zav of two sightings, who saw at first, before his counting. And when he saw again three on the night of the eighth, since night is lacking time, these three combine with those first two and it is like one long impurity, and he brings one offering.
gershom:a11.1: And that which is taught “he does not bring” is about a zav who had three sightings at first, for he was already obligated in an offering, and now these later ones need not combine with the earlier ones; and since at the time he saw the later ones it is lacking time, he brings only one offering.
gershom:a12.1: About a zav who had two sightings at first, it is obvious that he brings, since they combine.
gershom:a13.1: This teaches us “specifically”: that they combine where he saw on the night of the eighth, since he is already outside his days of counting; and the reason they combine is that night is lacking time.
gershom:a14.1: But if he saw on the seventh day, within his days of counting, they do not combine and he does not bring.
gershom:a15.1: As he holds: any sighting that negates [the count of his days of purity] does not combine to bring him to an offering. For we say there that [one who] saw on the seventh negates only that day, and he adds one day in its place.
gershom:a16.1: And let him teach this with “five bring one offering for many transgressions”: that is, this one too brings one offering for many discharges.
gershom:a17.1: It is not definitive for him to teach this, for Rabbi Yoḥanan said: If he saw one at night, on the night of the eighth day, and two on the eighth, he brings a second offering, since he saw the majority at a time fit to bring an offering.
gershom:a18.1: Know: that one at night and two by day combine and he brings. For the first sighting of a zav, if he did not see again, that one sighting has the law of mere semen, like one who had a seminal emission, which carries only impurity until evening.
gershom:a19.1: Yet if he saw two more, they combine for an offering.
gershom:a20.1: Are the cases comparable? One cannot derive it from there, since with the first sighting it is right that they combine, as he saw it at a time of liability, etc.
gershom:a21.1: But doesn’t Ḥizkiyya say: [If] a nazirite became impure on the eighth day of his purification, he brings another offering; on the night of the eighth, he does not bring another offering.
gershom:a22.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan says even: if he became impure at night, for he holds that night is not lacking time.
gershom:a23.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan needed to say: one at night and two by day, he brings an offering, etc.; lest you say, etc.
gershom:a24.1: A woman who has an uncertainty of five births: uncertain whether she gave birth, or uncertain whether it was an offspring.
gershom:a25.1: Or an uncertainty of five discharges: uncertain whether she saw three discharges before her menstrual period or within the eleven days between one period and the next, when she is one who watches a day [for a day] and not a zava.
gershom:a26.1: She brings one offering: out of uncertainty, and she is permitted to eat offerings.
gershom:a27.1: And the remaining: the other offerings are not an obligation for her to bring, since they were uncertain births.
gershom:a28.1: But if she had five definite births or five definite discharges, she brings one offering and eats offerings, and the remaining are an obligation for her to bring.
gershom:a29.1: There was an incident where nests, of women after childbirth and of zavot, stood in Jerusalem at a gold dinar per nest, because they had said “the remaining are an obligation for her.” Many women who had five definite births and definite discharges came, and many bought, and they made the nests expensive.
gershom:a30.1: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: This abode. He swore by the One who rested His name in this House: “I will not lie down tonight until I lower [the price of] the nests, until they stand at silver dinars.” And he entered the court in the Chamber of Hewn Stone and taught: A woman, etc., brings one offering for the others among them, and eats offerings and is exempt, and the remaining are not an obligation for her. And the nests became cheap because of this ruling, and that day they stood at rivatayim, at half a silver dinar, for in their language and in the language of the baraita they call half a dinar a ribua. [The Davidson English renders “one-quarter.”]
gershom:a31.1: Five definite births and five uncertain births: so it is written in the Tosefta, and this is more reasonable.
gershom:a32.1: She brings two nests, one for the definite, etc., and no more.
gershom:a33.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri says: For the definite she should say explicitly, “I am bringing it for the last,” and she is exempt from the others. And for those that are uncertain, if there is one definite birth or discharge among them, she says, “I am bringing it for the definite,” and is exempt from the rest.
gershom:a34.1: For Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri, who says “for the last,” compares them to a sin offering: one who is liable for five sin offerings, until he brings all of them; and in the end, when he completes the last, he is atoned. Here too it is no different: she brings for the last, and they are all like one long impurity, and it is as if she brought an offering for all of them, and she is atoned.
gershom:a35.1: And Rabbi Akiva, who says “for one of them,” whichever she wishes, compares them to immersions: one who is obligated in five immersions, once he has immersed one time he is purified. Here too it is no different. And they disagree about this verse: “And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be pure” [Leviticus 12:8].
gershom:a36.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri holds that “and she shall be pure” speaks of the sin offering; therefore he compares them to sin offerings. And Rabbi Akiva holds that “and she shall be pure” speaks of immersion; therefore he compares them to immersions.
gershom:a37.1: [The printed text marks: up to here belongs to 8a.] “If one who is obligated in five provisional guilt offerings”: they are compared to provisional guilt offerings because provisional guilt offerings come for an uncertainty, like these; and since they are divided with regard to guilt offerings, he must bring a provisional guilt offering for each one. Here too she should have to bring for each uncertain birth.
rashi:b2.1: Five provisional guilt offerings [etc.] … We are concerned for negligence: if they did not require her to say “I am bringing it for the last,” she would think that she was exempted by this offering and that the rest are not an obligation for her, and she would be negligent and not bring them. But when she is required to say “I am bringing it for the last,” she knows that the rest are an obligation for her. But for the uncertain, where the rest are not an obligation for her, we do not trouble her to say “I am bringing it for the last.”
rashi:b2.2: And Rabbi Akiva is not concerned for negligence: And I heard [another explanation]: “we are concerned for negligence,” lest she be negligent and not bring even one offering, and eat sacrificial food in bodily impurity. And it is very difficult for me. First: is it possible that she brings her offering, and yet, because she is not required to say “for the last,” we should be concerned that she will retract? And further: if you are concerned for that, all the more so with the uncertain she is lenient; so why is she not required to say “for the last,” lest she retract and not bring it, and eat sacrificial food in uncertain bodily impurity?
rashi:b4.1: Mishna. Four lacking atonement: they bring a sin offering, not for a sin, but in order to eat sacrificial food.
rashi:b6.1: Until the blood is sprinkled for him: for he must bring an offering, as is explained below.
rashi:b6.2: And a nazirite, for his wine, his shaving and his impurity: and a nazirite lacks atonement, for as long as he has not achieved atonement he is forbidden wine, shaving and becoming impure for the dead.
rashi:b7.1: Gemara. That he counts them as two: that he reckons zav and zava as two of those who lack atonement.
rashi:b8.1: From his flesh: from the force of his organ and the strength of his desire.
rashi:b8.2: A zava becomes impure by accident: as we say in the chapter Benot Kutim (Nidda 36b): “And if a woman has a discharge of her blood” [Leviticus 15:25]; here [a discharge by] accident is stated.
rashi:b8.3: And he becomes impure by sightings: if he saw three in one day.
rashi:b8.4: As by days: if he saw on three consecutive days, as is explained in Bava Kamma, chapter two (24a): a zava becomes impure only by days.
rashi:b10.1: There are two here: for “the leper” implies both male and female becoming impure through leprous marks.
rashi:b11.1: This is our reading: “If so, why does the verse state ‘man’? … to the matter below”: for [it cannot come] for the impurity of leprous marks itself, since “and the leper” is stated.
rashi:b11.2: “Man”: which is written in the upper verse, [is applied] to the matter of the lower verse, where letting the hair grow wild and rending are written, last, to tell you: a man lets his hair grow wild and rends his garments.
rashi:b12.1: The essence of their impurity is distinct: this one by sightings and by days, and that one by days and not by sightings.
rashi:b12.2: A split bean: for that is the measure of a leprous mark, half a bean.
rashi:b14.1: Ultimately, a nazirite: what is the reason he does not teach it? It is to permit him! And it answers: that is not to permit him sacrificial food but non-sacred wine, and when he reckons atonement, it is atonement that holds back some eating of sacrificial food.
rashi:b16.1: A convert is precluded from partaking of sacrificial meat: for even the Rabbis hold like Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, that he brings it to be permitted; and the reason [the first tanna] does not teach him is that he is not called “lacking atonement.”
rashi:b16.2: He brought one young bird: one young pigeon, in the morning.
rashi:b16.3: He may partake of sacrificial meat in the evening: provided that he brings the second, as we say below: to bring [only] one young bird is impossible.
rashi:b16.4: Here both of them are burnt offerings: as we say below in the Gemara (Keritot 9a), from the generation of the wilderness.
rashi:b17.1: He brought his obligation from an animal: one burnt offering; he has fulfilled it.
rashi:b17.2: A burnt offering and a peace offering: not precisely; rather, because he wants to teach “a meal offering and a peace offering, he has not fulfilled.”
rashi:b18.1: Just as you, a burnt offering and a peace offering: as it is written: “And he sent the young men of the children of Israel,” etc. [Exodus 24:5].
rashi:b19.1: It should not be enough for him: until he brings a peace offering.
rashi:b21.1: That is entirely for the Lord: from which the priest receives no benefit. For with an animal burnt offering, its hide goes to the priests, but with a bird burnt offering there is nothing.
tosafot:b12.1: Both this and that are a split bean: It could have said in the same way that zav and zava are distinct, since this one is with red and that one with white.
tosafot:b19.1: A bird was included, etc.: This is puzzling: let the zav and zava prove [otherwise], for whom a bird was included and not an animal.
gershom:b1.1: Rather, everyone compares them to immersions, and they disagree about whether we are concerned for negligence. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri, who says she should say “for the last” and be exempt, does so because he holds that we are concerned for negligence. For if you say she should say “for one of them” and be exempt, perhaps there is a woman who will give birth once, definitely, and will not want to bring an offering, saying: “Last year I had five definite births and I did not bring an offering for four of them”; and now too she does not bring an offering for this birth, and she is negligent and does not bring it. But when we say she should say “for the last,” she thinks: the reason they obliged me to say “for the last” is that it is all under the name of one birth, and it implies that the last atoned for all of them; so now too I am not exempt without an offering.
gershom:b2.1: And Rabbi Akiva, who says “for one of them,” holds that we are not concerned for negligence: since she knows that last year she was not exempted without any offering, now too she is not exempt, and she will bring an offering.
gershom:b4.1: Four who lack atonement: they may not eat sacrificial food until they bring their atonement, even though they have become pure.
gershom:b5.1: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov says: A convert, even though he has been circumcised and has immersed, lacks atonement, and is forbidden to eat sacrificial food until he brings his nest and the blood is sprinkled for him.
gershom:b6.1: And a pure nazirite who has completed his naziriteship is permitted to eat sacrificial food, since he is pure; but he lacks atonement with regard to wine, for he is forbidden to drink wine, to shave and to become impure for the dead until he brings his atonement.
gershom:b7.1: Becomes impure by accident: if he saw a discharge due to illness, or due to those things for which a zav is examined.
gershom:b9.1: And he becomes impure by sightings: by three sightings.
gershom:b10.1: As by days: like a zava by days, since “his discharge” is written three times of the zav.
gershom:b11.1: And a zava, by days: “And a woman, if she has a discharge… many days” [Leviticus 15:25]: “days” is two, “many” is three.
gershom:b12.1: And a zava becomes impure by accident: since “from her flesh” is not written of her. And that which is written, “And a woman, if she has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood” [Leviticus 15:19], speaks of a menstruating woman; and from this “in her flesh” we derive that she becomes impure [by blood] inside as [by blood] outside.
gershom:b13.1: When it says “and the leper,” there are two here: the “leper” above and this “and the leper” are two, one for a man and one for a woman.
gershom:b14.1: If so, what need is there to say “man”? The verse removed it, for the law of letting the hair grow wild and rending, from the matter below, from the unqualified “and the leper,” which implies [a woman too], and gave it to the leper above, of whom “man” is written: a man lets his hair grow wild and rends his garments. That is why “his garments” and “his head” are written in the masculine. Another version: if so, since from “leper” we derive man, woman and minor alike, why is “man” written? For the matter below, to tell you, etc.
gershom:b15.1: And not outside her tent: so that if she is a leper and her husband is not a leper, he is permitted to have relations with her.
gershom:b16.1: Zav and zava, the essence of their impurity is distinct: for a zav is by sightings and a zava by days. But a male leper and a female leper, their impurity is not distinct, since for both the measure of their impurity is a split bean.
gershom:b17.1: And Rabbi Eliezer holds that a convert brings an offering both to qualify him to enter the congregation and to qualify him to eat sacrificial food, as we say below in the baraita, “A convert is precluded from eating sacrificial food”; and that unattributed [baraita] is Rabbi Eliezer.
gershom:b18.1: And the nazirite too: now, since he needs an offering to permit him wine, even though it is non-sacred, even so he teaches it in our mishna.
gershom:b19.1: And according to Rabbi Eliezer, who teaches a nazirite even though he does not need to be permitted sacrificial food but only non-sacred [wine], let him also teach an impure nazirite, who needs an offering to permit him wine. Rabbi Eliezer holds that when an impure nazirite brings an offering, he does not bring it to permit him wine, but so that he will be fit for a naziriteship of purity to take effect upon him, as it is written, “But the former days shall be void” [Numbers 6:12]; and he is forbidden wine until he completes the naziriteship of purity. Therefore he does not teach an impure nazirite.
gershom:b20.1: Until he brings his nest: two young birds.
gershom:b21.1: If he brought one in the morning, he eats sacrificial food in the evening, and he may bring the other even after some time.
gershom:b22.1: If he brought his obligation from an animal: even one animal, as a burnt offering, he has fulfilled it; or two animals, a burnt offering and a peace offering, he has fulfilled it.
gershom:b23.1: And they said a nest, two young birds, only to be lenient with him; but if he wishes to bring an animal, he may bring it.
gershom:b24.1: Just as you: when you entered the covenant and the mitzvot, with a burnt offering and peace offerings, as it is written, “And he sent the young men of the children of Israel,” etc. [Exodus 24:5].
gershom:b25.1: For a bird: nests were included in order to be lenient, as we say below.
gershom:b26.1: For an animal burnt offering: one; all the more so.
gershom:b27.1: The verse restricted: “so he shall do”; and there, there was no meal offering.
gershom:b28.1: You must say: this is a bird burnt offering. For with an animal burnt offering its hide goes to the priests, whereas with a bird even its crop and feathers are forbidden for benefit, since they are absorbed in their place.
